title: Echo Hills Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Echo Hills wells have a 305-foot median depth, 7 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $25,800-$42,500.
h1: Echo Hills Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land or a home in Echo Hills means dealing with mountain bedrock, not a predictable shallow aquifer. Records for permitted wells within five miles show a 305-foot median depth and a 7.0 gallons-per-minute median reported yield. The middle half of wells runs from 190 to 471 feet deep and produces 4.0 to 10.0 gpm.

Those figures describe nearby permit records, not a guarantee for a particular lot. Echo Hills sits near Pine Valley, Upper Witter Gulch, Upper Bear Creek, Floyd Hill, Blue Valley, and Evergreen. Use the records to set expectations, then have a driller review the exact parcel, access, geology, permit requirements, and neighboring well history.

sections.heading: How deep are wells around Echo Hills?
sections.html:
Echo Hills wells commonly require substantial drilling through fractured mountain bedrock, identified on most permits as unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifer. The median completed depth is 305 feet. The middle half falls between 190 and 471 feet, so a bid based only on the median can miss a meaningful part of the local range.

Depth records are spread out: 9% are under 100 feet, 35% are 100 to 300 feet, 42% are 300 to 600 feet, and 15% reach 600 feet or more. The deepest recorded well is 3,523 feet. For a buyer, that spread matters when comparing drilling estimates. Ask for a per-foot rate, a realistic target depth, casing and grout assumptions, and the cost if the first target does not produce enough water.

sections.heading: What yield can a well make here?
sections.html:
Among nearby records that report pump yield, the median is 7.0 gpm, with the middle half between 4.0 and 10.0 gpm. Most reported wells fall in the 5 to 15 gpm range, representing 62% of the records. Another 28% produce 1 to 5 gpm, while 2% are under 1 gpm and 9% exceed 15 gpm.

A 7.0 gpm result is a useful local planning reference, but it is not a promise of sustained supply. A well's usable storage, recovery, pump setting, pressure tank, and household demand all matter. Have the driller explain the test method and ask how a low-yield result would affect the proposed home, livestock, irrigation, or backup storage.

sections.heading: What does the water table show in Echo Hills?
sections.html:
Static water-level records show a median depth to water of 90 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 46 to 150 feet. Only 182 wells in the nearby records report a static water level, so this is a smaller dataset than the depth and yield summaries.

The decade series rises from 29 feet below surface in the 1960s to 64 feet in the 1970s and 88 feet in the 1980s. It then measures 81 feet in the 1990s, 100 feet in the 2010s, and 100 feet in the 2020s. That pattern suggests water was measured deeper in the more recent records than in the 1960s, although the changing locations and limited measurements do not prove a uniform decline across Echo Hills. Confirm current conditions at the parcel.

sections.heading: Who has drilled near Echo Hills, and when?
sections.html:
Permit activity is heaviest in older records. The countywide nearby dataset shows 90 permits from the 1950s, 180 from the 1960s, 1,213 from the 1970s, 761 from the 1980s, 1,131 from the 1990s, 555 from the 2000s, 251 from the 2010s, and 136 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The most active drillers named in these records are James Drilling Company (Keaton, Michael K.) with 609 records, Walton with 391, and Living Water Systems Inc. (Goble, Robert) with 306. These counts reflect permit records, not recommendations or current availability. Before hiring anyone, verify the contractor's current licensing and insurance, request recent references, and check whether the proposed work fits Colorado DWR permit conditions.

sections.heading: What does a new well cost in Echo Hills?
sections.html:
Fractured granite and gneiss make drilling cost sensitive to depth and difficult ground. The local cost model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 305-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $19,800 to $30,500. A finished system, including pump, tank, trenching, and electrical, is estimated at $25,800 to $42,500.

That range is a budgeting tool, not a fixed bid. Ask what happens if the hole must go deeper, if casing or grout requirements change, or if access requires additional excavation. Get the drilling price separated from pump equipment, pressure system, electrical service, trenching, water testing, and any treatment. On a mountain lot, driveway and site access can also affect the contractor's mobilization and installation plan.

sections.heading: What risks should an Echo Hills buyer check?
sections.html:
The nearby environmental inventory includes 25 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 1,631 historic mine features, and 8 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those locations do not establish contamination at a specific property, but they justify a site-specific water test and a review of nearby land uses, mine workings, drainage, and historic activity.

Low yield and dry holes remain practical risks in fractured bedrock because water-bearing fractures are unevenly distributed. Review neighboring well depths, yields, static levels, and construction details before relying on a seller's verbal description. Also plan septic and building locations early. The well, septic system, driveway, house, and repair access must work together, and Colorado DWR permitting and any required augmentation plan can affect what a household-use well may legally supply.

sections.heading: What should you do before buying or building?
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, not just the Echo Hills average. Search nearby DWR permits and compare wells in Pine Valley, Upper Witter Gulch, Upper Bear Creek, Floyd Hill, Blue Valley, and Evergreen only as supporting context. Look for local depth, yield, static-level, casing, and completion patterns. A nearby successful well is useful evidence, but fractured rock can change quickly across short distances.

For a purchase, make the contract review include the well permit, construction report, pump information, water-quality results, and a flow or recovery test when available. For a new build, have a licensed Colorado driller and septic professional evaluate access, siting, electrical needs, storage, and wastewater setbacks before finalizing the house location. Confirm the intended household use with Colorado DWR, especially if the property is in a basin where an augmentation plan is required.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Echo Hills, Colorado?
faq.a: Nearby permitted wells have a 305-foot median depth. The middle half runs from 190 to 471 feet, while 42% are 300 to 600 feet and 15% are 600 feet or deeper. Fractured granite and gneiss make individual results unpredictable, so use the local range to review a driller's per-foot estimate rather than treating 305 feet as a guarantee.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Echo Hills?
faq.a: The local model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 305-foot median depth, drilling the hole is estimated at $19,800 to $30,500. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $25,800 to $42,500. A deeper hole, difficult access, or added casing and grout can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Echo Hills wells produce?
faq.a: Reported nearby wells have a 7.0 gpm median yield, with the middle half between 4.0 and 10.0 gpm. Most are in the 5 to 15 gpm range. However, 28% report 1 to 5 gpm and 2% are under 1 gpm. Ask for the test details and confirm that storage and recovery match the planned household demand.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Echo Hills?
faq.a: Permit records do not prove that water at a specific Echo Hills property is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles are 25 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 1,631 historic mine features, and 8 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the actual well for appropriate contaminants, review nearby land and mine history, and use treatment only after the results identify a need.

faq.q: Is water getting deeper in Echo Hills wells?
faq.a: Reported static water levels were 29 feet below surface in the 1960s, 64 feet in the 1970s, 88 feet in the 1980s, 81 feet in the 1990s, and 100 feet in both the 2010s and 2020s. That suggests deeper recent measurements than in the 1960s, but only 182 wells report static levels, so it does not prove a uniform local decline.
